source_text: Quis igitur ista ordinauit? quis distribuit atque distinxit? quis numerum, qualitatem, formas, uitam dedit ? haec enim omnia per se ipsa bona sunt nec inuenitur, unde cuique naturae nisi ab omnium bonorum deo auctore tribuantur. non enim sicut chaos describere, uel quo modo insinuare etiam poetae solent informem quandam materiem sine specie, sine qualitate, sine mensuris, sine numero et pondere, sine ordine ac distinctione confusum nescio quid atque omnino expers omni qualitate, — unde illud quidam doctores graeci iiroiov uocant — non ergo sic isti hanc quam uocant terram tenebrarum insinuare conantur, sed omnino aliter longeque diuerse atque contrarie latus lateri adiungunt atque conliniant: naturas quinque numerant, distingunt, ordinant, qualitatibus propriis enuntiant nec eas desertas infecundasque esse permittunt, sed suis inhabitatoribus conplent eisque ipsis formas congruas et suis habitationibus adcommodatas adtribuunt et quod antecellit omnibus, uitam. haec tanta bona enumerare et ab auctore omnium bonorum deo aliena esse dicere, hoc est nec in rebus agnoscere tantum ordinis bonum nec in se tantum erroris malum.
thought_title: The ordered goods of the land of darkness
orientation: Augustine is examining Mani's description of the land of darkness and arguing that the goods Mani attributes to it cannot come from anywhere but God.
pass_a_gloss: Who therefore arranged these things? Who distributed and distinguished them? Who gave number, quality, forms, life? For all these things are good through themselves, and it is not found from where they are attributed to any nature except from God, the author of all goods. For not as they are accustomed to describe chaos, or in what way even the poets are accustomed to suggest a certain formless matter without form, without quality, without measures, without number and weight, without order and distinction, a confused I know not what and altogether devoid of all quality — from which certain Greek teachers call it iiroiov — not therefore in this way do these men try to suggest this which they call the land of darkness, but altogether otherwise and far differently and contrarily they join side to side and smear together: they count five natures, they distinguish them, they order them, they declare them with their own qualities, and they do not allow them to be deserted and unfruitful, but they fill them with their own inhabitants and to these very inhabitants they attribute forms suitable and adapted to their own dwellings, and what surpasses all things, life. To enumerate such great goods and to say that they are alien to God, the author of all goods, this is not to recognize in things so great a good of order nor in oneself so great an evil of error.

choices.why: Keeps the reflexive emphasis that these goods are good in their own right, not merely instrumentally.

choices.english: from God, the author of all goods
choices.why: Preserves the genitive 'of all goods' with 'author' as the governing noun, matching the Latin word order and emphasis.
rejected: from God the author of all good things
from the God who is author of all goods

choices.why: Renders 'quandam' as 'a certain' to keep the indefinite quality Augustine gives to the poets' chaos.

choices.english: they join side to side and smear together
choices.why: Keeps the physical, almost crude image of joining and smearing that Augustine uses to mock Mani's account.
rejected: they attach side to side and blend
they join flank to flank and mix

choices.english: so great a good of order
choices.why: Preserves the genitive 'of order' and the emphatic 'tantum' as 'so great,' matching the rhetorical climax.
rejected: such a great good of order

choices.english: so great an evil of error
choices.why: Parallels the previous phrase, keeping the genitive 'of error' and the emphatic 'tantum.'
rejected: such a great evil of error

pass_b_english: Who, then, arranged these things? Who distributed and distinguished them? Who gave them number, quality, forms, and life? For all these things are good through themselves, and no source is found from which they may be assigned to any nature except from God, the author of all goods. It is not as when poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or in whatever way they suggest a certain formless matter, without quality, without measures, without number and weight, without order and distinction—some confused thing utterly devoid of all quality, which certain Greek teachers call apoion. No, these people do not try to suggest their so-called land of darkness in that way at all, but in an entirely different, far divergent, and contrary manner: they join side to side and align them. They count five natures, distinguish them, arrange them, declare them by their own proper qualities, and do not leave them deserted and barren, but fill them with their own inhabitants, and to those inhabitants they attribute forms suited to them and adapted to their dwellings—and what surpasses all these, life. To enumerate such great goods and yet say they are alien to God, the author of all goods—this is to fail to recognize in things so great a good of order, and in oneself so great an evil of error.

problems.quote: It is not as the poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or to suggest a certain formless matter without form
problems.source_quote: non enim sicut chaos describere, uel quo modo insinuare etiam poetae solent informem quandam materiem sine specie
problems.why: English adds 'without form' not in source; 'sine specie' already rendered as 'without form' later, making redundant and distorting structure.
problems.fix: It is not as the poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or to suggest a certain formless matter
problems.ruling: 'sine specie' rendered twice as 'formless' and 'without form'; source has no second phrase, distorting structure

problems.quote: this is to fail to recognize in reality so great a good of order
problems.source_quote: hoc est nec in rebus agnoscere tantum ordinis bonum
problems.why: 'in rebus' means 'in things,' not 'in reality'; changes philosophical claim about things to epistemological claim about reality.
problems.fix: this is to fail to recognize in things so great a good of order
problems.ruling: 'in rebus' = 'in things'; 'in reality' shifts philosophical claim from things to epistemology

edits.old: It is not as the poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or to suggest a certain formless matter without form, without quality
edits.new: It is not as the poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or to suggest a certain formless matter, without quality

edits.old: this is to fail to recognize in reality so great a good of order
edits.new: this is to fail to recognize in things so great a good of order

fixed: Removed redundant 'without form' after 'formless matter'; source has 'informem quandam materiem sine specie' where 'informem' = formless and 'sine specie' = without form, so the first 'without form' was an addition not in the source.
Changed 'in reality' to 'in things'; source 'in rebus' means 'in things,' not 'in reality.'

problems.quote: It is not as the poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or to suggest
problems.source_quote: non enim sicut chaos describere, uel quo modo insinuare etiam poetae solent
problems.why: Latin 'uel quo modo' means 'or in whatever way,' not 'or to suggest'; the infinitives depend on 'sicut,' comparing how poets describe chaos.
problems.fix: It is not as when poets are accustomed to describe chaos, or in whatever way they suggest
problems.ruling: 'uel quo modo insinuare' = 'or in the way [they] suggest'; English 'or to suggest' drops 'quo modo,' obscuring the comparison.

problems.quote: there is no source from which they could be attributed to any nature except from God
problems.source_quote: nec inuenitur, unde cuique naturae nisi ab omnium bonorum deo auctore tribuantur
problems.why: 'Unde' with passive 'tribuantur' means 'from which source they may be assigned/attributed,' but 'attributed to any nature' reverses the dative; 'cuique naturae' is the recipient, not the thing attributed.
problems.fix: and no source is found from which they may be assigned to any nature except from God
problems.ruling: 'unde cuique naturae...tribuantur' = 'from which they may be granted to each nature'; English reverses dative, saying attributed 'to any nature' as source.

Corrected 'there is no source from which they could be attributed to any nature except from God' to 'no source is found from which they may be assigned to any nature except from God' to reflect the passive 'tribuantur' and dative 'cuique naturae'.

problems.quote: they join side to side and smear together
problems.why: 'conliniant' (conlinere/colline, 'align/draw in line') is not 'smear'; sense is they set side by side and align (their two lands bordering).
problems.fix: they set side against side and align them
problems.ruling: conliniant is collineant (collineo), ‘align’, not conlino ‘smear’; latus lateri adiungunt is set side by side.

edits.old: they join side to side and smear together
edits.new: they join side to side and align them

fixed: conliniant fixed: 'smear together' to 'align them' — latus lateri adiungunt atque conliniant means setting the two lands side-by-side and aligning them, not smearing

last_rejected.why: 'Conliniant' means 'they plaster/cement together,' i.e., join seamlessly; 'smear' implies messy daubing, wrong sense.
last_rejected.fix: they join side to side and plaster them together
last_rejected.ruling: conliniant = 'smear/daub together'; 'smear' is within normal range, not a meaning change

last_rejected.quote: For all these things are good through themselves
last_rejected.source_quote: haec enim omnia per se ipsa bona sunt
last_rejected.why: 'Per se ipsa' means 'in themselves' or 'by their very nature,' not 'through themselves' which suggests causation.
last_rejected.fix: For all these things are good in themselves
last_rejected.ruling: 'per se ipsa' = 'through themselves' is valid rendering; no causation implied in context

last_rejected.quote: a certain formless matter, without quality
last_rejected.source_quote: informem quandam materiem sine specie, sine qualitate
last_rejected.why: The privation list drops sine specie (“without form”), a distinct item after formless matter.
last_rejected.fix: a certain formless matter, without form, without quality, without measures
last_rejected.ruling: "sine specie" (without appearance/form) is largely redundant with "informem" (formless), which is translated; omitting one item in a list of privations is minor and doesn't change meaning.
